what: OR Royalties owns royalties and streams on mines rather than mines themselves. It pays mining companies money upfront in exchange for a share of future production or revenue from a mine, and then collects that share for the life of the asset without paying operating or capital costs.
customers: It has no customers in the ordinary sense. Its counterparties are mining companies who want financing, and its income is a share of the metal they produce, sold at market prices. Its anchor asset is a royalty on the Canadian Malartic mine in Quebec.
money: Gold and silver royalties, dominated by a long-life Canadian gold mine.
Royalties on other metals and interests in development-stage projects.
moat: The royalty model is structurally superior to mining: the holder gets the upside when metal prices rise and when the miner expands the deposit, without ever paying for a cost overrun, a labour dispute or a new piece of equipment. Royalties also last the life of the mine and often cover ground the operator has not yet explored, so the asset can grow without the owner spending anything.
risks: Free cash flow was about negative $105.5M, because buying new royalties is an investment that shows as a cash outflow before any income arrives.
Revenue is concentrated in one principal asset, so an operational problem at that mine affects a large share of income.
The shares trade at about 15.4 times sales and 23.2 times earnings, a premium that reflects the quality of the model rather than cheapness.
Royalty companies compete to buy assets, and paying too much for a royalty is the only real way to destroy value in this business.
Only four analysts cover the stock, so the $43.50 average target rests on minimal coverage.
opportunities: Net margin of about 74% shows the model clearly: there are almost no costs between revenue and profit.
Revenue has grown from $183.2M in 2023 to $277.4M in 2025 as underlying mines expanded and metal prices rose.
Royalty holders benefit from exploration success at no cost: if the operator finds more ore, the royalty covers it.
No debt reported, which means the balance sheet carries none of the risk that periodically destroys mining companies.
Gold prices feed almost directly to the bottom line because the cost base barely moves.
watch: New royalty and stream acquisitions, and the price paid for them. Existing royalties take care of themselves; the only way management adds or destroys value is in what it buys and what it pays.
view: The royalty model is the best structure in mining and it is worth being precise about why. A mine owner faces rising labour costs, equipment failures, permitting delays, environmental liabilities and capital overruns, and keeps whatever is left after all of them. A royalty holder receives a fixed share of the revenue or the production and pays for none of it. When the gold price rises, the royalty holder gets the full benefit while the miner’s costs rise too. When the operator spends money to expand the deposit, the royalty covers the new ounces at no cost to its owner. That asymmetry is structural, not cyclical.

The 74% net margin is simply that model showing up in the accounts. There is almost nothing between revenue and profit because there is almost nothing to pay for. It is also why these companies trade at multiples that look absurd against mining peers — 23 times earnings for OR Royalties against single digits for many miners — and why that comparison is not meaningful. You are not buying the same thing.

The specific weaknesses here are concentration and scale. OR Royalties is small compared with Franco-Nevada or Wheaton, and a large share of its income comes from one principal Canadian asset. That is a genuine risk: a royalty on a mine with an operational problem produces nothing, and there is no diversification to absorb it. Smaller royalty companies also compete for new assets against larger ones with cheaper capital, which pushes them toward paying more or buying lower-quality royalties.

Which is exactly where the only real management decision in this business lies. Existing royalties need no management at all — they simply pay. Value is created or destroyed entirely in what gets bought and at what price, and that is the discipline to assess. The negative free cash flow is not a warning sign here; it is the company buying future income. Whether it bought well will not be visible for years, which is why the acquisition record, rather than this quarter’s revenue, is the thing to judge.
bull: Gold prices hold or rise while operators expand the deposits underneath existing royalties at no cost to OR, and new royalties are bought at prices that earn their keep.
bear: Concentration in one principal asset meets an operational problem, or competition for new royalties pushes management into overpaying for lower-quality ones.
